title: What Affects Transpiration?
question: How does one environmental change affect modeled plant water loss, and how does water reach the air?

blocks.prompt: Required before setup: For your selected environmental change, predict whether the changed plant will lose more or less water than the reference plant. Explain your reasoning.
blocks.text: The selected change may alter water loss through the leaf. I expect the result to depend on vapor movement or stomatal opening under the stated conditions.

blocks.prompt: Required before setup: Why compare one factor at a time and keep leaf area, water supply, temperature and time matched? Why must soil evaporation be blocked, and why compare mass changes instead of final masses alone?
blocks.text: Change one environmental factor while matching leaf area, water, temperature and time. Block soil/pot evaporation, keep the module off the pan, and compare each final mass with its own initial mass.
Timing: Before setup or balance observations. Selected factor: Airflow: still air → gentle moving air.

Two supplied daytime plant models have matched leaf area of 100 cm² and enough water. Air and leaf temperature stay at 25°C. Reference conditions are still air, 50% relative humidity and moderate daytime light. Change only your chosen factor at the other station. Relative humidity describes how close air is to saturation at its temperature. Pot/cover starting masses differ; compare each station with its own initial mass.

The enlarged section is supplied explanatory anatomy, not microscopy. Liquid reaches wet mesophyll walls; evaporation supplies vapor to leaf air spaces, and net vapor diffusion through stomata reaches outside air. The model omits cuticular loss and other real responses.

blocks.prompt: The changed station has the larger final mass. Does that prove it lost less water?
blocks.text:
No. Compare each final mass with that station’s own initial mass, then use the same time interval.
Correct! Different starting pot/cover masses can give different final masses. Water loss is initial minus final mass. Rate is that loss divided by the model interval. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: What normally passes from the leaf air spaces through an open stoma during transpiration?
blocks.text:
Water vapor; evaporation has changed liquid water into gas at wet internal cell surfaces.
Correct! Water evaporates from wet mesophyll surfaces into leaf air spaces. Vapor then diffuses through stomata and the air near the leaf. Guard cells regulate pores; they do not pump out liquid water. Revised after feedback.

blocks.prompt: What does this model comparison support?
blocks.text:
A result under its stated constant settings; real plants need further measurements and may regulate stomata differently.
Correct! This model isolates one factor and omits stress, feedback and several mass changes. In real studies, replication, controls and measurement limits matter. Correct on first recorded check.

These masses and settings are invented model data, not measurements from real plants. Each balance includes the plant, pot, soil and cover. The controller stays off the pan. An ideal seal blocks soil/pot evaporation. Water loss has a constant rate. It depends on the vapor difference and how easily vapor passes through pores and nearby air. Values are chosen for this lesson, not fitted to a species. Settings stay fixed for 30 model minutes. Brighter light opens stomata more without warming the leaf here. Wind changes nearby air; humidity changes the vapor difference. Real plants can respond differently, especially under stress or strong wind. The model leaves out growth, changes in stored water, gas exchange, drainage, leaks and air pushing on the balance. It also leaves out water loss through the waxy leaf coating. Real mass-loss estimates need these limits checked. Drawings are enlarged, not to scale. Vapor symbols explain invisible gas; they are not droplets. No physical weighing or plant-handling protocol is supplied.
